title: The Case of the Books Nobody Wanted
story: The library's weeding list is built from loan counts and it names four hundred books that have not gone out once in two years. Every one of them is on the top two shelves. Four explanations have been offered and each describes a real effect. Old books do go out less, and the sample is older than the collection average by about six years. Dull covers are a real deterrent, and the list is heavy with plain cloth bindings. Subject matters, and poetry and reference always lend less than fiction. The catalogue mislabels some of these books, and a book nobody can find is a book nobody borrows. Those four together might explain a lower rate, and the figure here is not lower but zero. The top shelf is two metres and ten centimetres from the floor. The step stool was taken away in September two years ago after a pupil fell from it. Ninety-four percent of all loans since then have come from below one metre fifty. A librarian ran a different measurement last month and counted the dust-free tops of the pages. The high shelves show sixty-one books with worn page edges and broken spines, all borrowed heavily before the stool went. A loan count does not measure what people want to read. It measures what people can reach.
question: Why have four hundred books never been borrowed?

suspects.who: 📏 The height the books sit at
suspects.why: the top shelf is two metres and ten centimetres from the floor and the step stool was taken away two years ago
old books do go out less, and the sample is older than the collection average by about six years
dull covers are a real deterrent, and the list is heavy with plain cloth bindings
poetry and reference always lend less than fiction
the catalogue mislabels some of these books, and a book nobody can find is a book nobody borrows

answer: The books are on shelves nobody has been able to reach since the stool went.
proof: “Ninety-four percent of all loans since then have come from below one metre fifty.”
“The high shelves show sixty-one books with worn page edges and broken spines, all borrowed heavily before the stool went.”
“A loan count does not measure what people want to read.”
clears: Age: “older than the collection average by about six years.”
Covers: “the list is heavy with plain cloth bindings.”
Subject: “poetry and reference always lend less than fiction.”
The catalogue: “a book nobody can find is a book nobody borrows.”
explain: Four real reasons a book lends less, and the list is not of books that lend less but of books that never lend at all. Nothing about a cloth binding produces a clean zero. The wear on the page edges is a second measurement of the same question, taken a different way, and it says these books were loved until the day the stool was removed.

title: The Case of the Salad Nobody Chose
story: The kitchen's uptake count says eleven pupils out of six hundred take the salad option, and the governors want it dropped. Four reasons have been given for the figure and each of them is a genuine problem with that salad. It costs twenty pence more than the pasta, which the kitchen's own pricing trial showed matters. It is served in a plain white bowl at the cold end of the counter, which is bad presentation by anybody's standard. The portion is smaller than the hot options by weight. And teenagers do pick hot food over cold in winter, which the county survey confirms. Those four would depress a figure and they would not flatten it to eleven. The salad is made in a single tray of about forty portions. The kitchen serves from half past eleven, and the tray is empty by seven minutes past twelve. The uptake count is taken from the till report at the end of service at twenty to one. Every pupil who wanted salad after seven minutes past was served something else and counted as something else. A tally kept at the counter for one week found a hundred and ninety pupils who asked for salad and were told it had gone.
question: Why does the count say eleven?

suspects.who: ⏰ The count taken after the salad ran out
suspects.why: the tray is empty by seven minutes past twelve and the count is taken at twenty to one
it costs twenty pence more than the pasta, which the kitchen's own pricing trial showed matters
it is served in a plain white bowl at the cold end of the counter
the portion is smaller than the hot options by weight
teenagers do pick hot food over cold in winter, which the county survey confirms

answer: The salad sells out long before the count that says nobody wants it.
proof: “The salad is made in a single tray of about forty portions.”
“Every pupil who wanted salad after seven minutes past was served something else and counted as something else.”
“A tally kept at the counter for one week found a hundred and ninety pupils who asked for salad and were told it had gone.”
clears: The price: “which the kitchen's own pricing trial showed matters.”
The presentation: “it is served in a plain white bowl at the cold end of the counter, which is bad presentation by anybody's standard.”
The portion: “smaller than the hot options by weight.”
The season: “teenagers do pick hot food over cold in winter, which the county survey confirms.”
explain: The figure of eleven is wrong in a way no arithmetic catches, because eleven really is what the till recorded. The till can only record what the kitchen had to sell. A tray of forty cannot produce a number above forty however many people want one, and the counter tally found a hundred and ninety of them.

title: The Case of the Brand That Snapped Most
story: The breakage book says Haleby pencils break four times as often as Corwin pencils, and the school is about to stop buying Haleby. Four differences between the brands are offered and all four are real. Haleby leads test softer on the laboratory scale, and a softer lead does break more readily. Haleby barrels are round and Corwin barrels hexagonal, and a round pencil rolls off a desk. The Haleby batch was delivered in August and stored in the damp cupboard, which weakens the glue along the seam. And Haleby pencils are two centimetres shorter, which changes how hard a hand can press before the lead gives. Those four together might account for a difference of a third, not of four times. Haleby pencils are issued to Years Seven and Eight and Corwin pencils to the sixth form. The breakage book is filled in by the stock cupboard when a class asks for replacements. Sixth formers buy their own replacements from the shop rather than asking. A fortnight of marked pencils, fifty of each brand given to the same Year Eight class, ended with nine Haleby and seven Corwin broken. The book never compared two brands. It compared two age groups and one habit of asking.
question: Do Haleby pencils really break more?

suspects.who: 🧑‍🎓 Who each brand was given to
suspects.why: Haleby pencils are issued to Years Seven and Eight and Corwin pencils to the sixth form
Haleby leads test softer on the laboratory scale, and a softer lead does break more readily
Haleby barrels are round and Corwin barrels hexagonal, and a round pencil rolls off a desk
the Haleby batch was stored in the damp cupboard, which weakens the glue along the seam
Haleby pencils are two centimetres shorter, which changes how hard a hand can press

answer: The two brands went to different year groups with different habits.
proof: “The breakage book is filled in by the stock cupboard when a class asks for replacements.”
“Sixth formers buy their own replacements from the shop rather than asking.”
“A fortnight of marked pencils, fifty of each brand given to the same Year Eight class, ended with nine Haleby and seven Corwin broken.”
clears: The lead: “a softer lead does break more readily.”
The barrel: “a round pencil rolls off a desk.”
The cupboard: “which weakens the glue along the seam.”
The length: “which changes how hard a hand can press before the lead gives.”
explain: Haleby pencils are genuinely the weaker pencil, by about a third, which the marked fortnight shows. The book says four times because it counts requests rather than breakages, and the group that never requests anything is the group holding the other brand. Put both brands in the same hands and the gap shrinks to almost nothing.

title: The Case of the Row That Cropped Best
story: The orchard record shows the north row yielding ninety kilograms a tree and the other four rows about thirty. The north row is to be propagated and the rest replaced. Four advantages of that row have been named and each is real. It faces south over open ground and gets about an hour more sun a day. It sits above the old stable yard, where the soil tests richer in nitrogen. It was planted three years earlier, so those trees are larger. And it is the only row on free-draining gravel rather than clay. Those four between them might be worth half as much again, not three times. The north row is picked by the head gardener with the orchard ladder. The other four rows are picked by classes on a Friday afternoon, without the ladder, for safety. A count made from the ground in October found fruit still hanging above two metres on every tree in rows two to five. Nine trees were picked properly by the gardener afterwards as a test, and they gave between seventy and eighty-eight kilograms. The record is not a measurement of what the trees grew. It is a measurement of what somebody could get down.
question: Is the north row really the best?

suspects.why: the north row is picked by the head gardener with the orchard ladder and the others by classes without it
it faces south over open ground and gets about an hour more sun a day
it sits above the old stable yard, where the soil tests richer in nitrogen
it was planted three years earlier, so those trees are larger
it is the only row on free-draining gravel rather than clay

answer: Only the north row is picked with a ladder.
proof: “A count made from the ground in October found fruit still hanging above two metres on every tree in rows two to five.”
“Nine trees were picked properly by the gardener afterwards as a test, and they gave between seventy and eighty-eight kilograms.”
“The record is not a measurement of what the trees grew.”
clears: The sun: “about an hour more sun a day.”
The soil: “the soil tests richer in nitrogen.”
The older trees: “those trees are larger.”
The drainage: “free-draining gravel rather than clay.”
explain: Four genuine advantages, worth perhaps half as much again, against a record that says three times. The ladder is not an advantage of the trees at all, and the fruit left hanging above two metres is the missing two thirds. Replacing those rows would have destroyed four healthy rows on the strength of a safety rule.

title: The Case of the Shed Where Nothing Was Stolen
story: The bike shed log records two thefts in three years and the school is citing it to refuse a request for cameras. Four reasons for the low figure have been offered and every one of them is true of that shed. It is overlooked by the staff room window for most of the day. The frame is bolted into concrete and the hoops are the sort a cutter struggles with. The gate is locked from nine until three. And most pupils use a good lock, which a spot survey put at seventy-one percent. Those four would lower a theft rate, and they would not take it to two. The log is written up from forms handed in at the school office. The office closes at four o'clock and the shed empties between half past three and six. A pupil who finds a bike gone at half past five comes back the next morning to an office with a queue, and most do not bother. The local police were asked for their own figures last month. They hold nineteen reports of bicycles taken from that address in the same three years. Seventeen of the nineteen are timed after four o'clock.
question: Why does the log show only two thefts?

suspects.why: the office closes at four o'clock and the shed empties between half past three and six
the shed is overlooked by the staff room window for most of the day
the frame is bolted into concrete and the hoops are the sort a cutter struggles with
the gate is locked from nine until three
most pupils use a good lock, which a spot survey put at seventy-one percent

answer: Thefts happen after the only place that records them has shut.
proof: “The log is written up from forms handed in at the school office.”
“They hold nineteen reports of bicycles taken from that address in the same three years.”
“Seventeen of the nineteen are timed after four o'clock.”
clears: The window: “overlooked by the staff room window for most of the day.”
The frame: “the hoops are the sort a cutter struggles with.”
The gate: “the gate is locked from nine until three.”
Locks: “which a spot survey put at seventy-one percent.”
explain: Every protection named here works during the day, and the log only exists during the day, so the log is a record of the hours the shed is safe. The police figures cover the same address and the same three years and are nearly ten times higher. Two is not a theft rate. It is an opening time.

title: The Case of the Tank That Killed Fish
story: Tank B has lost thirty-one fish in two years and tank A has lost four, and the club wants tank B stripped down. Four faults in tank B have been named and every one is real. Its heater runs a degree and a half warm, which the thermometer confirms. Its filter is the older model and turns the water over more slowly. It stands near the door and gets a draught whenever the room is used. And its gravel has never been replaced, so it holds more waste than tank A's. Those four would raise a death rate and they would not multiply it by eight. Tank B is the quarantine tank, and every fish bought for the club spends its first three weeks in it. Tank A receives only fish that have already survived those three weeks. A newly bought fish carries the stress of transport and whatever it arrived with, and the trade's own figure for first-month losses is about a quarter. Two hundred and ten fish have passed through tank B and sixty-eight through tank A. Thirty-one of two hundred and ten is fifteen percent, and four of sixty-eight is six. The gap is real and it is a third of the size the raw counts suggest.
question: Why does tank B lose so many fish?

suspects.who: 🚪 Tank B being the quarantine tank
suspects.why: every fish bought for the club spends its first three weeks in tank B, and tank A receives only survivors
its heater runs a degree and a half warm, which the thermometer confirms
its filter is the older model and turns the water over more slowly
it stands near the door and gets a draught whenever the room is used
its gravel has never been replaced, so it holds more waste than tank A's

answer: Tank B holds every new fish and tank A holds only the ones that lived.
proof: “Tank A receives only fish that have already survived those three weeks.”
“Two hundred and ten fish have passed through tank B and sixty-eight through tank A.”
“Thirty-one of two hundred and ten is fifteen percent, and four of sixty-eight is six.”
clears: The heater: “its heater runs a degree and a half warm, which the thermometer confirms.”
The filter: “turns the water over more slowly.”
The draught: “gets a draught whenever the room is used.”
The gravel: “holds more waste than tank A's.”
explain: Counting deaths without counting fish is the first error, and it accounts for most of the gap. The second is deeper: tank A's fish were selected by tank B. Every weak fish died before it could be an A statistic, which is why the healthiest tank in the room is the one that never meets a new arrival.

title: The Case of the Flavour That Outsold the Rest

The rota tells the bakers how many of each to make, and it asked for two hundred and forty chocolate and forty-five lemon. Two hundred and ten of two hundred and forty chocolate cakes sold, which is eighty-eight percent. Forty of forty-five lemon cakes sold, which is eighty-nine percent. The lemon table was cleared and packed away forty minutes before the sale ended. Twenty-two people were turned away from the lemon table in that forty minutes, which a helper counted on the back of a receipt. A count of what sold cannot tell you what would have sold, unless you also know what there was.

title: The Case of the Mittens That Were Always Wool

The site team's standing instruction, written in two thousand and nine, treats synthetic gloves as having no resale value. A fortnight of logging everything that entered the box, with nothing discarded, recorded fifty-one wool and thirty-eight acrylic. The audit was never a list of what was lost. title: The Case of the Recipe That Never Failed

title: The Case of the Bulbs That Failed Too Often
story: The maintenance file records sixty-one LED failures and nine filament failures this year, and the school is reverting to filament bulbs. title: The Case of the Clock That Was Never Wrong
story: The checking book for the tower clock carries eleven years of weekly entries and not one records an error above thirty seconds. The clock is being left out of the restoration on the strength of it. Four reasons for genuine accuracy have been offered and each is fair. It was rebuilt in nineteen ninety-eight with a new escapement. Its pendulum hangs in a sealed case, which keeps the dust and most of the damp off it. The tower holds a steady temperature because of the stone. And it is wound every Sunday by the same person, which keeps the drive even. Those four would make it a good clock, and eleven years without a single entry over thirty seconds is better than a good clock. The book is filled in by the winder on Sunday mornings. title: The Case of the Garden Full of Robins

title: The Case of the Pianists Who Were Better at Maths
story: The school's figures show pupils who learn the piano scoring eleven points above the year average in maths, and a bid is being written to fund piano lessons for everybody. Four mechanisms have been proposed and each has some research behind it. Reading two staves at once trains the handling of two streams of information. Rhythm is counted in fractions, and pupils who count them daily meet them early. Practice builds a habit of returning to something difficult. And performance teaches work under pressure. Those four are real and the published effect for each is small. Piano lessons at this school cost eighteen pounds a week and are arranged privately by families. Ninety-one percent of the pupils learning piano are not eligible for free school meals, against sixty-two percent of the year group. When the same figures are compared within the group that pays for lessons, the piano gap falls to two points. The county ran a funded scheme in two thousand and nineteen giving free lessons to a randomly chosen hundred pupils. That cohort finished one point above its control group. Learning the piano is mostly a measure of being able to afford to learn the piano.

title: The Case of the Kites That Never Met Bad Weather
story: Four years of club records show the field's wind running between eight and forty kilometres an hour and never outside it, and a member is writing that the site has unusually steady weather. Four reasons have been offered and each is physically real. The field sits in a shallow bowl with rising ground on three sides. The line of poplars along the western edge breaks the strongest gusts. The site is twelve kilometres inland, away from coastal extremes. And the valley runs across the prevailing wind rather than along it. Those four would narrow a range and they would not put a hard floor and a hard ceiling on it. The readings are taken by whoever turns up, from the handheld meter in the clubhouse. Nobody drives to a kite field on a still day, because there is nothing to do there. Nobody drives to a kite field in a gale either, because the club rules forbid flying above forty. The parish council's own weather station, four hundred metres away, logs every hour whether anybody is there or not. It records winds below eight on a hundred and ninety days a year and above forty on thirty-one. The club measured its own attendance rules.

the line of poplars along the western edge breaks the strongest gusts

the valley runs across the prevailing wind rather than along it

title: The Case of the Lucky Corner of the Field
story: The club's find book records sixty-one four-leaf clovers from the top corner of the field and nine from everywhere else, and the corner is being fenced as a conservation plot. Four reasons have been offered and each is a real possibility. The corner is the only part of the field that was never ploughed. It is damper, lying at the foot of the slope where water collects. It is mown less often because the mower cannot turn there. And disturbance is known to raise the rate of the mutation that produces a fourth leaflet. Those four could raise the local rate, perhaps by half. The find book records clovers found and has no column for time spent looking. The corner is where the club meets, because it is the only shaded spot and the gate is there. A log kept last summer recorded searcher-hours as well as finds. The corner took a hundred and forty hours of searching and the rest of the field took eleven. Sixty-one finds in a hundred and forty hours is one every two and a quarter hours, and nine finds in eleven hours is one every one and a quarter. Measured by the hour, the corner is the worst ground on the field.
question: Is the top corner really luckier?

the corner is the only part of the field that was never ploughed
it is damper, lying at the foot of the slope where water collects

disturbance is known to raise the rate of the mutation that produces a fourth leaflet

“The corner took a hundred and forty hours of searching and the rest of the field took eleven.”
“Measured by the hour, the corner is the worst ground on the field.”

The damp: “lying at the foot of the slope where water collects.”
The mowing: “the mower cannot turn there.”
Disturbance: “raise the rate of the mutation that produces a fourth leaflet.”

Once the hours go in, the corner falls from seven times better to nearly half as good. The club would have fenced off its own meeting place and called it a discovery.

title: The Case of the Flooding That Started in Two Thousand and Nineteen
story: The site record shows four flooding incidents in the yard before two thousand and nineteen and seventy-one since, and a drainage contract worth ninety thousand pounds is being prepared. Four causes have been offered and each is real. The playground was resurfaced in two thousand and eighteen with a tighter asphalt that takes water less readily. The new bicycle store covers a hundred and ten square metres that used to be grass. Rainfall at the parish station has risen about eight percent across the same period. And a new kerb line directs water that used to run onto the verge back towards the yard. Those four would raise a flooding rate and nobody is arguing they have not. The online estates form was introduced in January two thousand and nineteen and can be filled in from a phone in two minutes. Before that, a flood had to be reported by telephone to a county office open between ten and three. The caretaker's own diary, kept continuously since two thousand and eleven, mentions standing water in the yard in every year of its record. The diary counts between nine and fourteen floods a year throughout, with no step in two thousand and nineteen. The site record changed in that year. The yard did not.
question: Did the flooding really start in two thousand and nineteen?

the playground was resurfaced with a tighter asphalt that takes water less readily
the new bicycle store covers a hundred and ten square metres that used to be grass
rainfall at the parish station has risen about eight percent across the same period
a new kerb line directs water that used to run onto the verge back towards the yard

“The caretaker's own diary, kept continuously since two thousand and eleven, mentions standing water in the yard in every year of its record.”
“The diary counts between nine and fourteen floods a year throughout, with no step in two thousand and nineteen.”
clears: The resurfacing: “a tighter asphalt that takes water less readily.”
The bicycle store: “a hundred and ten square metres that used to be grass.”
More rain: “risen about eight percent across the same period.”
The kerb: “directs water that used to run onto the verge back towards the yard.”

A record that steps the moment the reporting method changes is describing the method, and the diary, which never changed, shows a flat line straight through the year everything supposedly began.

title: The Case of the Bed That Grew Everything Best
story: Bed four has produced the heaviest crop in each of six years and the garden club wants the other five beds rebuilt to match it. Four advantages have been named and each is genuine. It is the only raised bed, so its soil warms earlier in spring. It was filled with bought compost where the others use the school's own. It faces south-west and catches the afternoon sun. And its timber sides keep the rabbits out, which the chewed rows elsewhere confirm. Those four are worth real weight and the gap is more than two to one. Bed four stands beside the outside tap. The hose reaches bed four without being dragged and reaches bed five only if the coil is unwound across the path. The watering rota has one instruction on it, which is to water what needs it, and it is carried out by whoever is free at the time. A log kept last summer recorded eighty-one waterings for bed four and between nine and nineteen for the other five. Bed two was moved next to the tap in September as a test and grew the heaviest crop this year. Bed four was moved to the far end and came fourth.
question: Is bed four really the best bed?

it is the only raised bed, so its soil warms earlier in spring
it was filled with bought compost where the others use the school's own
it faces south-west and catches the afternoon sun
its timber sides keep the rabbits out, which the chewed rows elsewhere confirm

answer: Bed four is the bed the hose reaches, so it is the bed that gets watered.
proof: “A log kept last summer recorded eighty-one waterings for bed four and between nine and nineteen for the other five.”

“Bed four was moved to the far end and came fourth.”
clears: Being raised: “its soil warms earlier in spring.”
The compost: “where the others use the school's own.”
The aspect: “catches the afternoon sun.”
The sides: “which the chewed rows elsewhere confirm.”

The three whites that lay best in the run average five point two eggs a week, which is the number the commercial unit uses as its cut.

title: The Case of the School Where Everybody Walked

It gathered a hundred and forty responses from a roll of eight hundred and ten. The club meets to campaign about transport, and joining it is a choice pupils make. A gate count run by the office for five mornings in November, which counts everybody arriving by any means, found three hundred and nine arrivals by car. question: Do ninety-one percent really walk?

title: The Case of the Camera That Was Brilliant in the Dark
story: The club's portfolio holds forty low-light photographs, every one of them sharp, and the camera is being recommended for the trip on that evidence. The portfolio is assembled each term from whatever members choose to submit. The card from the November evening shoot was still in the bag and held nine hundred and six frames. Two hundred and forty of them are low-light and fourteen were submitted. A count of the two hundred and forty found a hundred and ninety-one too blurred to use and thirty-five visibly noisy. The camera's hit rate in low light is about six percent, and the portfolio's hit rate is a hundred. Nobody deleted anything dishonestly, and the weak frames simply were not worth submitting to a portfolio. A folder of successes cannot tell you anything about a rate unless somebody kept the failures.

title: The Case of the Compost That Grew Giants

The method sheet says to thin each tray to the strongest twelve seedlings at two weeks. Tray C was thinned on the fourteenth day as written. Trays A, B and D were not thinned, because the pupil responsible was away and nobody picked it up. Thinning also leaves the plants that remain with more root room and more light. Tray C's average is the average of twelve chosen plants and tray A's is the average of all forty-one that came up. The twelve tallest plants in tray A average twenty-nine centimetres. Thinning a tray does not make plants grow. It changes which plants are in the number at the end.
question: Is tray C's compost really better?

tray C's compost tests higher in nitrogen by a fifth
it holds water better on the laboratory's own measure
its texture is finer, which suits a small seed
it is pasteurised, so it carries fewer fungal spores

proof: “Tray C's average is the average of twelve chosen plants and tray A's is the average of all forty-one that came up.”
“The twelve tallest plants in tray A average twenty-nine centimetres.”
“Thinning a tray does not make plants grow.”
clears: The nitrogen: “higher in nitrogen by a fifth.”
Water: “holds water better on the laboratory's own measure.”
The texture: “which suits a small seed.”
Pasteurising: “it carries fewer fungal spores.”
explain: Tray C's compost is better, by about two centimetres, which is what the matched comparison gives. The other ten came from a step in the method that was carried out in one tray and missed in three. An average over a group that has had its weakest members removed is not comparable to an average over a group that has not.

title: The Case of the Flavour That Was Always Vanilla

title: The Case of the Balloons That All Landed in Towns
story: Two hundred balloons were released with reply cards and sixty-three came back. Fifty-eight of the sixty-three were found in towns and villages, and the report concludes that the prevailing wind carries balloons towards settlements. Four reasons have been offered and each sounds sensible. Towns sit in valleys, and the valley wind does funnel along them. Buildings and street trees catch a descending balloon where open ground lets it skip. The town lies downwind of the launch field on most days. And warm air rising over a town is known to affect how a light object descends. Those four might tilt a distribution a little. A card can only come back if a person finds the balloon, reads the card, and posts it. Towns hold most of the people, so towns are where found balloons are found. The moorland downwind of the launch field holds four houses in eleven kilometres. The club walked a measured transect across eleven kilometres of moorland downwind three days after the launch. It recovered twenty-nine balloons, none of which had been reported by anybody. A hundred and thirty-seven balloons were never heard of again, and the moor is the only place anyone has looked for them.
question: Do balloons really land in towns?
